newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Joint attack takes Afghan airbase, Masood says.
newsitem.headline: Joint attack takes Afghan airbase, Masood says.

text.p: The ousted Afghan government said it staged a joint attack with its newfound ethnic Uzbek allies and drove the Taleban militia out of the important Bagram military airbase near Kabul on Friday.
"They were operating together in mixed units. They attacked from the north and northeast," a senior official at the headquarters of government military commander Ahmad Shah Masood told reporters.
"Now we have control of all of the airport at Bagram, the main part of the Taleban force has retreated along the new road back towards Kabul," said the official, Mirabbuddin Astana.
Masood's men previously controlled about half the airbase, 60 km (40 miles) north of Kabul, with the Taleban Islamic militia, which seized the Afghan capital last month, holding the other half.
Astana said Masood's men fought side-by-side with fighters from Uzbek military commander Abdul Rashid Dostum's forces from northern Afghanistan, using tanks, artillery and mortars.

It was the first reported joint operation between Dostum's Jumbush troops and Masood's Jamiat soldiers, which have been enemies more often than not since the mujahideen came to power in Kabul in 1992.

Dostum sent a dozen tanks and several hundred men to join Masood on Thursday after formally recognising the government driven from Kabul and promising to back Masood if the Taleban did not stop fighting.
Reporters saw an intensive hour-long barrage against Taleban forces holding the important Bagram road junction about five km (three miles) from the airbase.
"We don't know about the junction," Astana said. "We have been firing heavy weapons into that area and we have just sent our infantry in to see if the Taleban are still there."
Masood earlier told Taleban fighters to quit the Afghan capital. "We want the Taleban to evacuate Kabul," Masood told Reuters in the town of Jabal os-Siraj north of the front line.
"A limited international force under U.N. supervision should control Kabul and pave the way for all-party talks on a broad-based government."
Masood, who won fame as a guerrilla leader against Soviet troops in the 1980s, said the alternative was war.

Earlier in the the day the Uzbeks, descendants of the Mongols of Genghis Khan, were hit hard by mortar bombs that fell on their positions at the rate of one a minute at times south of Charikar, a 30-minute drive from Jabal os-Siraj.
They sought shelter behind natural and man-made fortifications in the foothills west of the main highway.
The Uzbeks held talks with Taleban leaders on Wednesday and Thursday, but there was no word on any outcome beyond a Taleban spokesman saying he was hopeful understanding could be reached.

A Taleban evacuation of Kabul was floated at the United Nations. The United States called it "probably premature", although State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said a proposal to demilitarise Kabul was "an important idea".
There was no immediate reaction from the Taleban on Friday, the Islamic day of rest, but they had rejected the earlier Masood ultimatum and vowed to defend Kabul.
